lactater estimates the lactate threshold concepts that are most used in sport science. This article says how each
one is defined, how lactater computes it, what the evidence says about it, and how to collect data that does the
methods justice. Every statement points to its source; where only an abstract was available, it says so.

## Two thresholds, many methods

Most authors describe the lactate response to a step test with two thresholds and three phases: a first rise of
lactate above resting values (LT1) and a second, abrupt increase (LT2), which split the intensities into three
zones with distinct metabolic, hormonal and cardio-respiratory responses (Hofmann & Tschakert, 2017). The methods in
lactater fall into the three families of a review that counted 25 lactate threshold concepts: fixed lactate
concentrations, a first rise above baseline, and concepts aimed at the maximal lactate steady state (MLSS) or a
distinct change in the curve (Faude et al., 2009).

| Method | Definition | Curve | Reference |
|---|---|---|---|
| Log-log | Crossing of two straight lines through log(lactate) vs log(intensity) | none (measured stages) | Beaver et al., 1985 |
| OBLA 2.0-4.0 | Intensity at a fixed lactate of 2.0 to 4.0 mmol/L | user's choice | Heck et al., 1985; Kindermann et al., 1979; Skinner & McLellan, 1980 |
| Bsln+ 0.5-1.5 | Intensity at 0.5 to 1.5 mmol/L above baseline | user's choice | Berg et al., 1990; Zoladz et al., 1995 |
| Dmax | Point on the curve furthest from the line between the first and last stage | 3rd degree polynomial | Cheng et al., 1992 |
| ModDmax | As Dmax, from the stage before the first rise of at least 0.4 mmol/L to the last stage | 3rd degree polynomial | Bishop et al., 1998 |
| Exp-Dmax | As Dmax, on an exponential plus constant curve | exponential | Hughson et al., 1987 |
| Log-Poly-ModDmax, Log-Exp-ModDmax | As Dmax, from the Log-log threshold | polynomial or exponential | Jamnick et al., 2018 |
| LTP1, LTP2 | Breakpoints of three straight lines through lactate vs intensity | none (measured stages) | Hofmann et al., 1997; Pokan et al., 1997 |
| LTratio | Lowest lactate / intensity ratio | B-spline | Dickhuth et al., 1999 |
| IAT | 1.5 mmol/L above the lactate at LTratio | B-spline | Dickhuth et al., 1999; Röcker et al., 1997 |

## How lactater computes them

**Fitted curves.** The 3rd and 4th degree polynomials are fitted by least squares. "B-spline" is a natural cubic
regression spline with 4 degrees of freedom. The exponential plus constant, `a + b * exp(c * x)`, is fitted by
searching `c` only, and only positive values as in Hughson et al. (1987): for a fixed `c` the model is linear in `a`
and `b`. This needs no starting values and cannot fail to converge. `lactate_fit_quality()` compares the curves on your data.

**Fixed concentrations (OBLA, Bsln+, IAT).** The intensity is found by solving the fitted curve for the target
lactate. When the curve crosses the target more than once (an early lactate dip), the highest crossing is used.
Bsln+ takes the resting sample as the baseline, or the first stage when there is no resting sample.

**The Dmax family.** Every variant takes the point where the fitted curve lies furthest *below* a straight line that
ends at the last stage. Where the line's ends sit differs between papers, and lactater follows each one by default
(`dmax_anchor = "original"`):

* Dmax and Exp-Dmax: on the curve, "the two end points of the curve" (Cheng et al., 1992; Jamnick et al., 2018).
* ModDmax: at the measured values, "the LT and the final lactate point" (Bishop et al., 1998).
* Log-Poly-ModDmax and Log-Exp-ModDmax: from the Log-log threshold on the curve to "the final lactate point"
  (Jamnick et al., 2018).

Other authors drew Dmax from the measured points too: "the two end data points" (Bishop et al., 1998), "the first
and last lactate measurements" (Bentley et al., 2007) or "the first and last measured points" (Heuberger et al.,
2018). `dmax_anchor = "fitted"` puts every end on the curve and `"observed"` every end at the measured values. On a
smooth curve the choice moves Dmax by less than 1 W; when lactate levels off in the last stage it can move a
threshold by tens of watts.

The ModDmax first rise is "at least 0.4 mmol/L" between two stages (Heuberger et al., 2018); Bishop et al. (1998)
and Jamnick et al. (2018) wrote "> 0.4", which differs only when two stages differ by exactly 0.4 mmol/L. Bishop et
al. measured plasma lactate from the fingertip. Change the rise with `moddmax_rise`, for example for sweat lactate.
The resting sample is never used, and the Log-log start of the Log-*-ModDmax variants is computed without it.

**Log-log.** Beaver et al. (1985) split the log-log data into two segments that share the stage between them, fitted
a straight line to each, and took the threshold where the two lines cross. They chose the split by eye; Jamnick et
al. (2018) took "the intersection point of the two lines with the lowest residuals sum of squares". lactater tries
every stage as the split, with at least three stages per line (a line through two points has no residuals, which
would favor the shortest segments), so Log-log needs at least five stages. When the two lines cross outside the
measured stages, the result is `NA`.

**LTP.** Hofmann et al. (1997) and Pokan et al. (1997) found each turn point as the crossing of two regression lines
"with minimal standard deviation", inside a window: LTP1 from the first lactate value up to 4 mmol/L (Hofmann) or
75% of the maximal power (Pokan), and LTP2 from LTP1 to the maximal power. Their tests had 1-min and 90-s stages,
so the windows held many samples. With the 6-8 stages of a typical step test the windows hold too few stages, so
lactater fits three connected straight segments to all stages at once, trying every pair of breakpoints with at
least two stages per segment. The result is the global optimum and never depends on starting values.
`ltp_fix_first_slope = TRUE` keeps the segment before LTP1 flat.

**Heart rate.** The heart rate at each threshold is interpolated between the measured stages.

## What the evidence says

The strongest evidence on validity comes from studies that compare a threshold with the MLSS measured directly.

* In 17 trained male cyclists who did five step tests (1, 3, 4, 7 and 10 min stages) and constant-power bouts to
  find their MLSS, Log-Poly-ModDmax from the 4-min stage test gave the best estimate of the MLSS (mean difference
  1.1 W, ICC 0.96). Dmax differed from the MLSS by 19 to 49 W, and OBLA 4.0 overestimated it in every test
  (Jamnick et al., 2018; single study, venous blood).
* In 48 male cyclists (24 on placebo, 109 tests), the intra-subject variation of the thresholds over five tests was
  3.4% for Dmax, 3.6% for IAT, 3.8% for the 4 mmol/L threshold, and 4.3% for modified Dmax. Modified Dmax predicted a
  time trial best (r = 0.94), with the 4 mmol/L threshold as a simpler alternative (Heuberger et al., 2018; single
  study, venous blood, Lactate Pro 2).
* A review concluded that LT1 has some evidence for separating the moderate and heavy exercise domains, but that
  most methods (other than critical power and critical speed) have little evidence for separating the heavy and
  severe domains. The same review lists test-retest variation for Dmax (3.8-10.3%), OBLA 4.0 (3.1-8.2%) and
  Bsln+ 0.5, 1.0 and 1.5 (1.2-3.7%, 3.4-12.6% and 3.1-3.4%), notes that the intensity of one athlete can differ by
  about 30% between methods, and that Bsln+ 1.5 estimated the MLSS in two studies with 3-min stages but not with
  other stage lengths (Jamnick et al., 2020; review).

Most of this evidence comes from trained, male, cycling populations; check how well it matches the athletes you test.

## Collecting good data

* **Stage duration** changes the thresholds: shorter stages can put the lactate threshold at a higher intensity (Bentley
  et al., 2007, review; Jamnick et al., 2018, compared stages from 1 to 10 min). Stages of at least 3 min have been
  recommended (Jamnick et al., 2020). Keep the protocol the same between tests of the same athlete.
* **Analyzer.** Portable analyzers had coefficients of variation of about 2-4% and mostly negative bias, largest above
  15 mmol/L; use the same unit for an athlete's repeated tests (Bonaventura et al., 2015).
* **Sampling site.** In cycling, fingertip and earlobe samples differed by 9.2% on average (95% of differences between
  -24.9% and 58.7%) without changing the prescribed power (Moran et al., 2012). Do not switch sites between tests.
* **Sample type.** Plasma lactate was about 50% higher than erythrocyte lactate, and capillary and venous whole blood
  also differed, so values from different sample types cannot be compared directly (Foxdal et al., 1990; 10 healthy
  men).
  Fixed-concentration methods (OBLA, Bsln+, IAT) assume blood lactate; `lactate_checks()` warns when `sample` says
  otherwise.

```{r}
results <- lactate_threshold(demo_data, intensity, lactate, heart_rate, plot = FALSE)
lactate_checks(results)
```

## Methods lactater does not include

* **Stegmann's IAT** draws a tangent to the lactate curve over time from the point in recovery where lactate falls
  back to its end-of-exercise value (Stegmann et al., 1981). It needs timed recovery samples, and some of its
  assumptions about lactate kinetics "have been challenged" (Faude et al., 2009).
* **Keul's and Simon's IAT** are the points where the curve's tangent reaches 51 and 45 degrees (Faude et al.,
  2009). An angle depends on how the axes are scaled, which only the original papers define, and they were not
  available to check.
